title: Vedanta Splits Into Five: Four Demerged Companies Hit the Stock Market on Monday. Here Is What NRI Investors Need to Know.
excerpt: The largest corporate demerger in Indian history reaches its final act as Vedanta Aluminium, Vedanta Oil & Gas, Vedanta Power, and Vedanta Iron & Steel begin trading on the BSE and NSE on June 15 — creating pure-play bets on India's commodity future.
body:
On Monday, June 15, four newly created companies will begin trading on the Bombay Stock Exchange and the National Stock Exchange, completing the most ambitious corporate restructuring in recent Indian market history. If you hold shares in Vedanta Ltd, you already own them — whether you planned to or not.

Vedanta Aluminium Metal Limited (VAML), Vedanta Oil and Gas Limited (VOGL), Vedanta Power Limited, and Vedanta Iron and Steel Limited (VISL) will each list separately after the National Company Law Tribunal approved the demerger scheme in December. The plan became effective on May 1, and every shareholder on record received one equity share in each of the four demerged companies for every one share held in Vedanta Ltd.

The result is a five-way split of the Anil Agarwal-led natural resources conglomerate into focused, sector-specific businesses — each with its own capital structure, management strategy, and investor proposition.

How the Listing Works

Both exchanges confirmed on June 11 that all four entities will debut through a special pre-open session under the "IPO and Other" category, designed to facilitate orderly price discovery before regular trading begins.

Here is the critical detail for traders: all four stocks will be placed in the Trade-for-Trade (T2T) segment for the first 10 trading sessions. Under this framework, every transaction must be settled through physical delivery of shares. Intraday trading — buying and selling within the same session — is not permitted.

The exchanges impose this restriction on newly listed stocks to curb speculative volatility and ensure genuine price discovery. For NRI investors accustomed to trading through overseas brokerage platforms, this means any buy or sell order will settle on a T+1 basis with mandatory delivery.

What Each Company Brings

The demerger separates Vedanta's operations into distinct commodity verticals, each with different risk profiles and growth trajectories:

Vedanta Aluminium Metal (VAML) houses the group's aluminium smelting and refining operations — India's largest. With global aluminium demand rising on the back of electric vehicle production and renewable energy infrastructure, VAML is positioned as a direct play on the energy transition.

Vedanta Oil and Gas (VOGL) inherits the group's exploration and production assets, including the prolific Rajasthan block. Oil and gas remains Vedanta's most profitable segment, though it carries geopolitical and commodity price risk that will now be isolated from the rest of the group.

Vedanta Power operates the Talwandi Sabo thermal power plant in Punjab, a 1,980 MW facility. It is the most straightforward of the four — a regulated power utility with predictable cash flows but limited growth upside.

Vedanta Iron and Steel (VISL) brings together the group's iron ore mining and steel operations, primarily in Goa and Karnataka. Steel demand in India is growing at 8-10 per cent annually, driven by infrastructure spending, but the segment faces margin pressure from Chinese overcapacity and fluctuating ore prices.

The Value Unlock Thesis

Vedanta's management has argued for years that the conglomerate structure obscured the true value of individual businesses. A diversified holding company trading at a discount to the sum of its parts is a familiar problem in Indian markets — and the demerger is the textbook solution.

Vedanta Resources CEO Deshnee Naidoo told investors during the company's most recent earnings call that the restructuring would "provide opportunities to global investors, including sovereign wealth funds, retail investors and strategic investors, with direct investment opportunities in dedicated pure-play companies linked to India's remarkable growth story."

The logic is sound in theory. Sector-focused companies attract specialist investors, command higher multiples, and access capital more efficiently than conglomerates. But the reality of five simultaneous listings — each finding its own price, its own shareholder base, and its own analyst coverage — is messy and unpredictable.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

For overseas Indians holding Vedanta through demat accounts or global brokerage platforms, several practical questions need answering before Monday:

Portfolio visibility. Check whether your broker has already credited the four new shares. Some platforms may take additional time to reflect demerged entities, especially if the shares are held through custodian chains.

Tax implications. The demerger is structured as a tax-neutral event under Indian law — the cost basis of the original Vedanta shares is apportioned across the five entities based on their relative fair market values. NRIs in the US should consult their tax advisors on how this apportionment affects capital gains reporting under IRS rules, particularly for PFIC (Passive Foreign Investment Company) classification.

Dividend policy. Vedanta has historically been one of the highest-yielding stocks on the Indian market, with a dividend yield exceeding 10 per cent. Post-demerger, dividend capacity will be distributed across five entities, and it remains unclear which companies will maintain aggressive payout policies. Oil and gas is the most likely candidate; power and iron & steel may prioritise debt reduction.

Liquidity risk. The T2T segment restriction means the first 10 sessions could see thin volumes and wide bid-ask spreads, especially in the smaller entities like Vedanta Power and VISL. Patience will be more valuable than speed.

Vedanta shares traded largely flat on Friday, opening 3 per cent higher at ₹314 before settling near ₹304 on the NSE. The market appears to have priced in most of the demerger's upside already — but the real repricing will happen only when each entity stands on its own and reveals what it is worth in isolation.

Monday will answer the first question. The next twelve months will answer the rest.

nri_angle: NRIs holding Vedanta shares through demat or overseas broker accounts will find four new stocks in their portfolios on Monday — understanding the listing mechanics, trade restrictions, and tax implications is essential before the first trade.
